standard.title: Experiment and play with visual conventions and materials
standard.description: experiment and play with visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can use play and imagination to discover possibilities with materials (AC9AVAFD01). They have begun noticing visual qualities and developing ideas through experimentation. They have not yet deliberately experimented with visual conventions as named elements.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students experiment and play with visual conventions, visual arts processes and materials, reflecting on what they discover.

nodes.label: Playing within limits
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can work with constraints on materials or processes to focus experimentation and notice what the material can do.
nodes.minimum_width: Work with one material or process constraint (e.g. only one colour, only folding and tearing) and describe what was discovered.
nodes.typical_width: Play with a range of constrained experiments (limited materials, limited tools, limited time, silent working); describe discoveries and failures; identify what could be used in a future artwork.
wider: Work in small groups to make something from a surprise bag of everyday materials — compare what different groups discovered about the same materials
Set a timed challenge to find as many ways as possible to create lines using a wide range of materials — compare results and discuss what each option is good for

response_modes.reason: Constrained play focuses attention on what materials actually do rather than defaulting to familiar habits. Different constraint types (colour, tool, process) reveal different material properties.

success_criteria: Engages with at least one material or process constraint
Describes at least one discovery — what worked, what failed, or what could be used again

nodes.label: Reflecting on experimentation
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use questions (Viewpoints-style) to reflect on their arts experiences — naming what was challenging, what was discovered and what failures led to something new.
nodes.minimum_width: Answer at least one reflection question about an experiment: what was challenging, what was discovered, or what failed and what came from the failure.
nodes.typical_width: Use Viewpoints questions to reflect on multiple experiments; document reflections through annotation, arrows or statements; connect discoveries to potential future artworks.
wider: Create a sound or voice file that accompanies a visual experiment — talk through the thinking and learning as a 'work-in-progress' presentation
Examine artworks and identify a 'layer + layer + layer' structure — experiment with the same layering approach and annotate how each layer changed the work
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who cannot reflect on their experiments cannot convert discoveries into purposeful future making — the reflective habit is the mechanism that links experimentation to growing artistic practice.

response_modes.reason: Reflection at this level is not intuitive — students need question scaffolds ('What was challenging?', 'What failed and what came from it?') to surface the thinking. Without the scaffold, reflection stays at 'I liked it/didn't like it'.

success_criteria: Responds to at least one reflection question about an experiment with specific content
Identifies something specific that was challenging, discovered or produced from failure

nodes.label: Using arts language
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can use visual arts language when describing and documenting their experiments — naming conventions, processes and effects.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least two visual arts terms (e.g. line, shape, texture, colour, layering) when describing an experiment or artwork.
nodes.typical_width: Use visual arts language accurately across multiple experiments; annotate visual experiments with short statements and arrows; identify open lines, closed shapes, layering and other conventions in their own work.
wider: Explore visual conventions in artworks by First Nations Australians — use visual arts language to describe what is observed with guidance from culturally authoritative resources
Identify the difference between open lines and closed shapes across a range of media — digitally fill selected areas using collaged closed shapes to form silhouettes

response_modes.reason: Accurate use of visual arts language requires repeated use across contexts until it becomes fluent. Students who use terms inconsistently or only when prompted need consolidation practice across many examples.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: First Nations visual arts contexts offer particularly rich vocabulary-building opportunities — colours, symbols and patterns not typically named in Western tradition expand the range of language students use to describe visual work.
success_criteria: Uses at least two visual arts terms accurately when describing an experiment or artwork
Applies at least one term to their own work in a way that shows they understand what it names
